subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Action]
passage: On his first evening in the hostel corridor, Dhruv knocked on the two doors next to his and said his name. On Tuesday he joined a study group in the common room, run by Ankita, a second-year who said the maths seminar was less scary in a crowd. He saved the warden's number and his local guardian's number on the first page of his phone and on a card in his wallet. Then he set a reminder: video call with Amma and Papa every Sunday at eight. When homesickness hit on Thursday night, he had somewhere to go. He texted the study group, played cards with the boy next door, and counted three days until Sunday. It wasn't perfect, but it was bearable.

qa.q: On which day and time did Dhruv schedule the calls home?
qa.a: Dhruv set the video call with Amma and Papa for every Sunday at eight.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling on Thursday night, and what helped?
qa.a: Dhruv felt homesick, and texting the study group, playing cards with the boy next door and counting three days until Sunday helped.

qa.q: What could Dhruv add if the homesickness lingers for a couple of months?
qa.a: He could speak with the warden or a counsellor, since these outlets work best alongside trained adults when a low mood does not ease.

qa.q: How might the boy next door see Dhruv's knock?
qa.a: The boy may feel welcomed and glad to have a friendly neighbour, since a hello on the first evening makes the corridor less lonely.

grounding: A newcomer greets hostel neighbours, joins a study group, saves the warden's and a guardian's numbers and schedules calls home so homesickness has outlets.

passage:
“Hi. I'm Yusuf, just moved into Room 14. Thought I'd say hello.”
“Ramesh, Room 15. Welcome. First time away from home?”
“First time. Honestly, the room's so quiet it's strange.”
“It gets better. A few of us study together in the common room, eight to ten. Physics tonight. Come.”
“I will. Also, where does the warden sit? I want to save the number.”
“Ground floor, by the gate. Everyone forgets to save it till there's a problem.”
“I've got my local guardian's number too, my uncle's friend in Kalyan Nagar. Saved it last night.”
“You're more organised than I was. I cried the whole first week.”
“I've fixed calls home for Wednesday and Sunday evenings. Ammi wanted daily. We compromised.”
Ramesh laughed. “Smart. Daily calls made me miss home more.”
“See you at eight, then?”
“Bring your formula sheet.”

qa.q: When does the study group meet?
qa.a: Eight to ten, in the common room.

qa.q: How is Yusuf feeling in the first days at the hostel?
qa.a: Yusuf feels a bit lonely, finding the quiet room strange, but hopeful and eager to settle in.

qa.q: Why is saving the warden's and guardian's numbers early a good step?
qa.a: If something goes wrong, help is one call away, instead of hunting for numbers in a panic.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see the new neighbour?
qa.a: Ramesh seems welcoming and a little impressed, remembering crying through his own first week.

grounding: Shows a newcomer greeting a hostel neighbour, joining a study group, saving the warden's and local guardian's numbers, and scheduling calls home.

subtopic: Moving to a new city for study
subtype: Approach: building a support network early [Action]
passage:
In my first week at the hostel in Pune, I made myself a rule: one new connection a day. I'm Rukmini, and I'd heard enough stories about people who stay in their rooms and cry till Diwali.
Day one, I knocked on the doors on either side and said hello; one neighbour lent me a bucket. Day two, I saved the warden's number and my local guardian's, Kavita Aunty in Kothrud, and stuck them on my cupboard. Day three, Sumit from my maths class said a few of them solved problems together in the library after dinner. I went, was useless, and they asked me back anyway.
I also fixed my calls home: Tuesday and Saturday, eight o'clock, half an hour. When I felt homesick in between, I wrote it in my diary instead of calling.
It still hurt some nights. But by the end of the month I had people to sit with at dinner.

qa.q: What did the neighbour lend Rukmini on day one?
How did Rukmini feel on some nights, even with the plan?
qa.a: Rukmini still felt homesick and hurt some nights, though less alone as the month went on.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini add if the homesickness got heavier?
qa.a: Talk to the warden or a counsellor, or visit Kavita Aunty on a weekend, so there is an adult nearby to lean on.

qa.q: How might Sumit see Rukmini joining the study group?
qa.a: Sumit likely sees a keen newcomer and is happy to include Rukmini, even if slow at first.

grounding: Shows a newcomer greeting hostel neighbours, joining a study group, saving the warden's and local guardian's numbers, and scheduling calls home.
